metadata.description: A DHCP address scope — a subnet's dynamic pool(s), options, and reservations. Grounded in the DHCP protocol concepts (RFC 2131 / RFC 8415). The concrete pool/option/lease model is provider config (any DHCP provider — Kea, dnsmasq, ISC DHCP, a cloud DHCP), projected not dictated; UDLM carries the neutral subnet + the graph edges. UDLM does not prescribe DHCP as the way to serve addresses — an address's origin is a field on Network.IPAddress (static/dhcp/link-layer/random).

zone.description: WHAT KIND OF NETWORK THIS IS — DMZ, management, internal, storage — as a governed TAXONOMY term (Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm), not a property bundle and not a floor. A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A REQUIREMENT, and the distinction is why this is a taxonomy where `tier` is reference data: a floor is something a second provider can MEET, a category is something a thing IS. Taxonomy is also the only one of the two that carries `normalization_rules`, which is what this needs — providers report `dmz-2`, `DMZ_RESTRICTED` and `dmz restricted`, and all three have to land on one canonical term before any policy can match on it. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Nothing critical hangs off a zone directly: it is not an authorization, not a control, and not a boundary. ANYTHING REQUIRED BECAUSE OF A ZONE IS ENFORCED BY POLICY READING IT — the model carries the classification, policy acts on it, which is the same split that governs everything else here. That also keeps the model on the right side of zero-trust architecture, which derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207); UDLM already ships a `zero_trust.posture` setting that a location-as-trust reading would contradict. ON THE BASE though it does not apply to every network type (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): enough of the family carries a category that the base is the right home, and an element that some types leave unpopulated is what `optional` is for. Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3) — a category two providers can both report is portable by definition. Provider-reported, like `tier`.

tier.description: HOW GOOD THIS NETWORK IS — a reference to a governed `network_tier`, exactly parallel to `storage_tier`. Each term DENOTES A FLOOR (bandwidth, latency), so asking for a tier is asking for the floor and any network meeting it qualifies: one provider's "10G" and another's "high-throughput" are interchangeable iff both clear it. That is what keeps the intent portable — the match is against the floor, never the string. NAME-SELECTABLE BUT REQUIREMENTS-AUTHORITATIVE (ADR-036, ruled 2026-07-27): a consumer may select by tier name, explicit requirements win where both are given, and the provider records its native class as a realized output rather than something the consumer had to know. ON THE BASE, NOT A TYPE, because performance is expected to be consumable by ALL network class providers and portable (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3), so the category base is where a fact every provider must report belongs. Provider-reported at registration or discovery — the party that knows is the one that says.

subnet.description: Scope subnet in CIDR (common-elements: cidr), e.g. 192.0.2.0/24.

pools.description: Dynamic allocation ranges within the subnet (DHCP).

reservations.description: DERIVED — not authored here. A projection of every Network.IPAddress(allocation: static) bound to a Hardware.NetworkInterface (its MAC) contained by a host (its hostname), within this scope. The reservation truth lives on the IPAddress records (DCM ADR-023); a DHCP provider renders its reservations/leases from this set.

relationships.name: dhcp_server_host
relationships.description: Host(s) running the DHCP server(s) serving this scope (e.g. an HA pair).

adopts.role: reference implementation — one DHCP provider's subnet/pool/reservation model (MPL-2.0, referenced by name only, not the type's grounding)

context.purpose: Declares a subnet's DHCP configuration — dynamic pools, options, lease time — as the neutral surface any DHCP provider serves.
context.plain_description: One subnet's DHCP setup: the required `subnet` CIDR, the dynamic ranges leased from — `pools` here (start/end pairs; the allocation-side Network.IPAddressPool calls its ranges `ranges`) — common `options` (router, dns_servers, domain_name), and `lease_time`. Reservations are not authored here — they are derived: every statically-allocated address record bound to an interface projects into this scope's reservation list, so the fact that an address belongs to a MAC lives in exactly one place. The DHCP server software is a provider; this record is what it renders its config from.
use_when: You need a subnet's dynamic ranges and options declared portably, independent of which DHCP server serves them.
You need static reservations to fall out of address records automatically instead of being maintained twice.
not_for: Allocation-side accounting of a range (who holds which address, is it exhausted) — Network.IPAddressPool; the scope is service-side config. The two overlap on ranges by design, and both document it.
One address or reservation — Network.IPAddress with static allocation; it projects into the scope.
works_with: Network.IPAddress — the address records whose static allocations project into reservations.
Network.AddressService — the operated service serving this scope.
Compute.BareMetalHost / Compute.VM — the servers the scope is served from.
